solutions.title: Choose entries one at a time

prompt: **Power Round, Problem 2a.** A *permutation* of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a listing $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ of $1,\dots,n$ in some order. It is also read as an *operation* on ordered listings: $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ sends the $\sigma(1)$th element to the first position, the $\sigma(2)$th element to the second position, and so on. Applying it to $(1,2,\dots,n)$ gives the listing $\sigma$ itself; the *identity* $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,n)$ does nothing. The *composition* $\sigma\circ\tau$ is the operation of performing $\tau$ first, then $\sigma$. The *inverse* $\sigma^{-1}$ is the permutation with $\sigma^{-1}\circ\sigma=\mathbf 1$. Compute the composition $\sigma\circ\tau$ of the permutations $\sigma=(1,5,4,3,6,2)$ and $\tau=(2,4,6,3,1,5)$.

solutions.title: Apply the operations in order
solutions.body:
First perform $\tau$ on $(1,2,3,4,5,6)$ to get the listing $(2,4,6,3,1,5)$. Then perform $\sigma$: the new $i$th entry is the $\sigma(i)$th entry of the old listing. With $\sigma=(1,5,4,3,6,2)$ the new entries are the old 1st, 5th, 4th, 3rd, 6th, 2nd entries: $2,1,3,6,5,4$.

**Answer: $(2,1,3,6,5,4)$**

solutions.title: Undo the operation
solutions.body:
The $m$th entry of $\sigma^{-1}$ is the position at which $m$ occurs in $\sigma$ (so that $\sigma^{-1}\circ\sigma=\mathbf 1$).

For $(3,1,4,2)$: $1$ is in position $2$, $2$ in position $4$, $3$ in position $1$, $4$ in position $3$, so the inverse is $(2,4,1,3)$. For $(2,4,6,3,1,5)$: the positions of $1,\dots,6$ are $5,1,4,2,6,3$, so the inverse is $(5,1,4,2,6,3)$.

**Answer: $(2,4,1,3)$ and $(5,1,4,2,6,3)$**

prompt: **Power Round, Problem 2c.** A *permutation* of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a listing $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ of $1,\dots,n$ in some order. It is also read as an *operation* on ordered listings: $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ sends the $\sigma(1)$th element to the first position, the $\sigma(2)$th element to the second position, and so on. Applying it to $(1,2,\dots,n)$ gives the listing $\sigma$ itself; the *identity* $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,n)$ does nothing. The *composition* $\sigma\circ\tau$ is the operation of performing $\tau$ first, then $\sigma$. The *inverse* $\sigma^{-1}$ is the permutation with $\sigma^{-1}\circ\sigma=\mathbf 1$. Show that $(\sigma\circ\tau)^{-1}=\tau^{-1}\circ\sigma^{-1}$ for all permutations $\sigma$ and $\tau$ of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$.
answer: $\tau^{-1}\circ\sigma^{-1}$ undoes $\sigma\circ\tau$ (use associativity)

solutions.title: Undo in reverse order
solutions.body: Composition of operations is associative (performing three operations in sequence does not depend on how we group them). Then $$(\tau^{-1}\circ\sigma^{-1})\circ(\sigma\circ\tau)=\tau^{-1}\circ(\sigma^{-1}\circ\sigma)\circ\tau=\tau^{-1}\circ\mathbf 1\circ\tau=\tau^{-1}\circ\tau=\mathbf 1.$$ So $\tau^{-1}\circ\sigma^{-1}$ satisfies the defining property of $(\sigma\circ\tau)^{-1}$. The inverse is unique: if $\rho\circ\pi=\mathbf 1=\rho'\circ\pi$ then $\rho$ and $\rho'$ agree on every listing of the form (arbitrary listing)$\circ\pi$, and as $\pi$ is a bijection of positions this is every listing, so $\rho=\rho'$. Hence $(\sigma\circ\tau)^{-1}=\tau^{-1}\circ\sigma^{-1}$. ∎

prompt: **Power Round, Problem 3.** A *permutation* of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a listing $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ of $1,\dots,n$ in some order. It is also read as an *operation* on ordered listings: $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ sends the $\sigma(1)$th element to the first position, the $\sigma(2)$th element to the second position, and so on. Applying it to $(1,2,\dots,n)$ gives the listing $\sigma$ itself; the *identity* $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,n)$ does nothing. The *composition* $\sigma\circ\tau$ is the operation of performing $\tau$ first, then $\sigma$. The *inverse* $\sigma^{-1}$ is the permutation with $\sigma^{-1}\circ\sigma=\mathbf 1$. Suppose that a process shuffles a deck in the order $\sigma$ into the order $\tau$. Which permutation will be produced when $(1,2,\dots,n)$ is shuffled by that same process? Justify.
answer: $\tau\circ\sigma^{-1}$

solutions.title: Process as an operation
solutions.body:
A (deterministic) shuffling process is an operation $\mu$ (a permutation of positions). Applying $\mu$ to a deck whose listing is $\sigma$ produces, by definition of composition, the listing $\mu\circ\sigma$ (first $\sigma$, then $\mu$). We are told $\mu\circ\sigma=\tau$. Composing with $\sigma^{-1}$ on the right (and using associativity and $\sigma\circ\sigma^{-1}=\mathbf 1$, valid because $\sigma$ is a bijection): $\mu=\mu\circ\sigma\circ\sigma^{-1}=\tau\circ\sigma^{-1}$.

Applying $\mu$ to the identity listing $(1,\dots,n)$ gives $\mu\circ\mathbf 1=\mu$. So the result is $\tau\circ\sigma^{-1}$.

**Answer: $\tau\circ\sigma^{-1}$** ∎

prompt: **Power Round, Problem 4.** A *permutation* of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a listing $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ of $1,\dots,n$ in some order. It is also read as an *operation* on ordered listings: $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ sends the $\sigma(1)$th element to the first position, the $\sigma(2)$th element to the second position, and so on. Applying it to $(1,2,\dots,n)$ gives the listing $\sigma$ itself; the *identity* $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,n)$ does nothing. The *composition* $\sigma\circ\tau$ is the operation of performing $\tau$ first, then $\sigma$. The *inverse* $\sigma^{-1}$ is the permutation with $\sigma^{-1}\circ\sigma=\mathbf 1$. The probability that a random shuffle turns a deck in the order $\sigma$ into the order $\tau$ is called the *transition probability* from $\sigma$ to $\tau$. For any random shuffle, show that the transition probability from $\sigma$ to $\tau$ is the same as the transition probability from $\mathbf 1$ to $\tau\circ\sigma^{-1}$.
answer: Both equal $P(\mu=\tau\circ\sigma^{-1})$ for the random operation $\mu$

solutions.title: Random operation
solutions.body: A random shuffle chooses a random operation $\mu$ on positions; its distribution does not depend on the labels of the cards (relabelling cards does not affect how the shuffle treats positions). Applied to a deck $\sigma$ it gives $\mu\circ\sigma$. Hence $$P(\sigma\to\tau)=P(\mu\circ\sigma=\tau)=P(\mu=\tau\circ\sigma^{-1})=P(\mu\circ\mathbf 1=\tau\circ\sigma^{-1})=P(\mathbf 1\to\tau\circ\sigma^{-1}).$$ ∎

answer: Reversing a permutation swaps ascents and descents

solutions.title: Reversal bijection
solutions.body: If $\sigma$ has $k$ ascents, it has $n-1-k$ descents (each of the $n-1$ positions is an ascent or a descent). The reversal $(\sigma(n),\dots,\sigma(1))$ turns an ascent $\sigma(i)<\sigma(i+1)$ into a descent (in the reversed order, the pair appears as $\sigma(i+1)>\sigma(i)$), and vice versa. So it has $n-1-k$ ascents. Reversal is its own inverse, hence a bijection between permutations with $k$ ascents and permutations with $n-1-k$ ascents. ∎

For example, $(2,7,1,3,5,4,8,6)$ has ascents at positions $1,3,4,6$ and descents at $2,5,7$. The *Eulerian number* $\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle$ is the number of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with exactly $k$ ascents. Using the recurrence $\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle=(k+1)\left\langle {n-1 \atop k}\right\rangle+(n-k)\left\langle {n-1 \atop k-1}\right\rangle$, compute a table of Eulerian numbers $\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle$ for $1\le n\le6$, $0\le k\le6$.

solutions.title: Apply the recurrence row by row
solutions.body:
Start with $\left\langle {1 \atop 0}\right\rangle=1$ and all other entries of row 1 equal to $0$. Then each entry is $(k+1)\cdot$(entry above) $+(n-k)\cdot$(entry above-left):

| $n$ | $k=0$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 4 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 11 | 11 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 26 | 66 | 26 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 6 | 1 | 57 | 302 | 302 | 57 | 1 | 0 |

For example $\left\langle {6 \atop 2}\right\rangle=3\left\langle {5 \atop 2}\right\rangle+4\left\langle {5 \atop 1}\right\rangle=3\cdot66+4\cdot26=302$. Each row sums to $n!$.

prompt: **Power Round, Problem 9.** An *ascent* of a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a position $1\le i<n$ with $\sigma(i)<\sigma(i+1)$; a *descent* is a position $1\le i<n$ with $\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)$ (every position $i<n$ is one or the other). For example, $(2,7,1,3,5,4,8,6)$ has ascents at positions $1,3,4,6$ and descents at $2,5,7$. The *Eulerian number* $\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle$ is the number of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with exactly $k$ ascents. Prove Worpitzky's Identity: $$x^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle\binom{x+k}{n}.$$ To ensure that the binomial coefficient makes sense, assume that $x$ is an integer and $x\ge n$.
answer: Induction on $n$ using the Eulerian recurrence

solutions.title: Induction
solutions.body:
Let $\binom{y}{m}=\frac{y(y-1)\cdots(y-m+1)}{m!}$ for any real $y$; both sides are polynomials in $x$, so it is enough to prove the identity as a polynomial identity (equality for all integers $x\ge n$ then follows). We use $\left\langle {0 \atop 0}\right\rangle=1$.

*Base case* $n=0$: $1=\left\langle {0 \atop 0}\right\rangle\binom x0$.

*Step.* Assume $x^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle\binom{x+k}n$. By the recurrence (with $\left\langle {n \atop -1}\right\rangle=\left\langle {n \atop n+1}\right\rangle=0$), $$\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}\left\langle {n+1 \atop k}\right\rangle\binom{x+k}{n+1}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(k+1)\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle\binom{x+k}{n+1}+\sum_{k=0}^{n}(n-k)\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle\binom{x+k+1}{n+1},$$ where in the second sum we shifted $k\to k+1$. Now $\binom{x+k}{n+1}=\binom{x+k}n\frac{x+k-n}{n+1}$ and $\binom{x+k+1}{n+1}=\binom{x+k}{n}\frac{x+k+1}{n+1}$. So the right side equals $$\sum_{k=0}^n\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle\binom{x+k}n\cdot\frac{(k+1)(x+k-n)+(n-k)(x+k+1)}{n+1}.$$ The numerator is $(k+1)x+(k+1)(k-n)+(n-k)x+(n-k)(k+1)=(n+1)x$, so the fraction equals $x$ and the sum is $x\cdot x^n=x^{n+1}$ by the induction hypothesis. ∎

solutions.title: Counting proof (outline)
solutions.body: For a positive integer $x$, count the $x^n$ functions $f:\{1,\dots,n\}\to\{1,\dots,x\}$ by sorting positions by value: each function determines a permutation $\sigma$ (positions ordered by increasing value, ties broken by position). A permutation with $k$ ascents is compatible with exactly $\binom{x+k}{n}$ functions (choose a weakly increasing sequence of values $v_1\le\dots\le v_n$ that is strictly increasing across each descent), and summing over permutations gives the identity.

prompt: **Power Round, Problem 10.** A *permutation* of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a listing $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ of $1,\dots,n$ in some order. It is also read as an *operation* on ordered listings: $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ sends the $\sigma(1)$th element to the first position, the $\sigma(2)$th element to the second position, and so on. Applying it to $(1,2,\dots,n)$ gives the listing $\sigma$ itself; the *identity* $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,n)$ does nothing. The *composition* $\sigma\circ\tau$ is the operation of performing $\tau$ first, then $\sigma$. The *inverse* $\sigma^{-1}$ is the permutation with $\sigma^{-1}\circ\sigma=\mathbf 1$. An *ascent* of a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a position $1\le i<n$ with $\sigma(i)<\sigma(i+1)$; a *descent* is a position $1\le i<n$ with $\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)$ (every position $i<n$ is one or the other). For example, $(2,7,1,3,5,4,8,6)$ has ascents at positions $1,3,4,6$ and descents at $2,5,7$. A *rising sequence* of a permutation $\sigma$ is a maximal sequence of consecutive numbers $k,k+1,\dots,l$ that appear in this order as a subsequence (not necessarily adjacent entries) of $\sigma$. Every permutation decomposes into disjoint rising sequences; for example $(6,1,2,4,7,5,3)$ has the three rising sequences $(1,2,3)$, $(4,5)$, $(6,7)$. Show that the number of rising sequences of a permutation $\sigma$ is equal to one more than the number of descents of $\sigma^{-1}$: $$\#\{\text{rising sequences of }\sigma\}=\#\{\text{descents of }\sigma^{-1}\}+1.$$
answer: $k$ and $k+1$ are in the same rising sequence iff $\sigma^{-1}(k)<\sigma^{-1}(k+1)$

solutions.title: Compare positions of k and k+1
solutions.body:
The $m$th entry of $\sigma^{-1}$ is the position of $m$ in $\sigma$; write $p(m)=\sigma^{-1}(m)$. The rising sequences partition $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into blocks of consecutive integers $k,\dots,l$ with $p(k)<p(k+1)<\dots<p(l)$, each maximal. So $k$ and $k+1$ lie in the same block iff $p(k)<p(k+1)$, i.e. iff $k$ is an ascent of $\sigma^{-1}$; and $k+1$ starts a new block iff $p(k)>p(k+1)$, i.e. iff $k$ is a descent of $\sigma^{-1}$.

The number of blocks is $1$ (the block containing $1$) plus the number of $k\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ at which a new block starts, i.e. $1+\#\{\text{descents of }\sigma^{-1}\}$. ∎

solutions.title: Count words

Summing over all $(j_1,\dots,j_a)$ counts every word of length $n$ exactly once, so $\sum\binom{n}{j_1,\dots,j_a}=a^n$ (this is the multinomial theorem for $(1+\dots+1)^n$). solutions.title: Words of drops
solutions.body:
The cards in each pile are dropped bottom first, so within a pile the relative order never changes. The final permutation is therefore determined by the *drop word* $w_1\cdots w_n$, where $w_t$ is the pile from which the $t$th dropped card came, and every word with $j_k$ letters $k$ is possible. Conversely the permutation determines the word (we know which pile each card belongs to). So the possible permutations correspond bijectively to such words: $\frac{n!}{j_1!\cdots j_a!}=\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}$ of them.

**Answer: $\binom{n}{j_1,\dots,j_a}$** ∎

prompt: **Power Round, Problem 15c.** For nonnegative integers $j_1+\dots+j_a=n$, the *multinomial coefficient* is $\binom{n}{j_1,\dots,j_a}=\frac{n!}{j_1!\,j_2!\cdots j_a!}$. Prove that, *given the initial cut*, every permutation of $1,\dots,n$ which is possible after the dropping stage occurs with equal probability. answer: Given the cut, each possible permutation has probability $\frac{j_1!\cdots j_a!}{n!}$; each path has probability $\frac1{a^n}$

solutions.title: Compute a drop-word probability
solutions.body:
Fix the cut $(j_1,\dots,j_a)$ and a possible permutation, i.e. a drop word. At each step the probability of dropping from pile $k$ is $J_k/(J_1+\dots+J_a)$ where the denominator is the number of cards still held. Over the whole process the denominators are $n,n-1,\dots,1$, giving $n!$. For pile $k$ the numerators at its successive drops are $j_k,j_k-1,\dots,1$, giving $j_k!$. Hence the probability of any possible permutation is $\frac{j_1!\cdots j_a!}{n!}=\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}^{-1}$, the same for all.

A path is a cut together with a resulting permutation. Its probability is $\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}\frac1{a^n}\cdot\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}^{-1}=\frac1{a^n}$. Different paths are different outcomes, so the probability of ending at $\sigma$ is the sum over paths ending at $\sigma$, i.e. $\frac{\#\{\text{paths to }\sigma\}}{a^n}$. ∎

solutions.title: Both parts
solutions.body:
(i) By Problem 15(c) every path of the GSR $a$-shuffle has probability $1/a^n$.

(ii) Suppose a shuffle has every path equally likely, with common probability $c$. The paths starting with the cut $(j_1,\dots,j_a)$ are in bijection with the possible drop words (Problem 15(b)), so there are $\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}$ of them and the cut has probability $c\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}$. Summing over all cuts and using $\sum\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}=a^n$ gives $c=a^{-n}$. So the cut probabilities are $\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}/a^n$ and, given the cut, each path has conditional probability $1/\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}$, which are exactly the GSR probabilities. ∎

answer: Given the cut, every possible permutation has probability $1/\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}$ in both shuffles

solutions.title: Show equal conditional probabilities
solutions.body:
Fix the cut $(j_1,\dots,j_a)$ and write $s_t=j_1+\dots+j_t$. Every merge preserves the relative order inside each pile, so the final permutations that can occur are exactly interleavings of the piles preserving each pile's internal order (and all of them can occur), the same set as for the standard $a$-shuffle.

Given such a final permutation $\pi$, the intermediate pile $M_t$ (after merging piles $1..t$) must be the subsequence of $\pi$ consisting of the cards of piles $1..t$ (merging later never reorders earlier cards). So the sequence of merges leading to $\pi$ is uniquely determined, and merge $t$ is one specific interleaving of $M_{t-1}$ (size $s_{t-1}$) with pile $t$ (size $j_t$). By Problem 15(c) with $a=2$ each interleaving has probability $1/\binom{s_t}{j_t}$. Thus $$P(\pi\mid\text{cut})=\prod_{t=2}^a\frac{j_t!\,s_{t-1}!}{s_t!}=\frac{s_1!}{s_a!}\prod_{t=2}^aj_t!=\frac{j_1!\cdots j_a!}{n!}=\binom n{j_1,\dots,j_a}^{-1}.$$ This equals the conditional probability for the standard $a$-shuffle (Problem 15(c)). As the cut distributions are the same, so are the probabilities of every permutation. ∎

solutions.title: Bijection of paths
solutions.body:
By Problem 15(c) (with relabelled cards, Problem 4) the standard $a$-shuffle's transition probability from $\tau$ to $\sigma$ is (number of paths $\tau\to\sigma$)$/a^n$; by 16(c)(i) the inverse shuffle's from $\sigma$ to $\tau$ is (number of its paths)$/a^n$. So it suffices to give a bijection between the paths.

An inverse-shuffle path from $\sigma$ to $\tau$ is an assignment of each card of $\sigma$ to one of $a$ piles such that stacking gives $\tau$. Let $P_k$ be the cards assigned to pile $k$, in the order they appear in $\sigma$ (bottom to top). Then $\tau=P_1P_2\cdots P_a$ (concatenated, pile $1$ at the bottom), and $\sigma$ is an interleaving of the sequences $P_1,\dots,P_a$ preserving their internal order.

A standard-shuffle path from $\tau$ to $\sigma$ is: cut $\tau$ into consecutive blocks $P_1,\dots,P_a$ (bottom block first), then drop to obtain $\sigma$, which is again an interleaving of $P_1,\dots,P_a$ preserving each block's internal order. The two descriptions have the same data: the block sequence $(P_1,\dots,P_a)$ with $\tau=P_1\cdots P_a$, and $\sigma$ an order-preserving interleaving of the blocks (equivalently, the assignment of each card of $\sigma$ to its block). Hence the paths correspond bijectively and the transition probabilities are equal. ∎

solutions.title: Combine the labels
solutions.body:
Give each card two independent uniform labels: $f\in\{1,\dots,a\}$ in the first shuffle and $g\in\{1,\dots,b\}$ in the second. An inverse $a$-shuffle is exactly a *stable sort of the deck by $f$* (cards with smaller $f$ go lower, cards with equal $f$ keep their relative order). The second inverse shuffle is a stable sort of the new deck by $g$ (labels $g$ assigned independently of the arrangement are again i.i.d. uniform for the cards). The composite is therefore the stable sort of the original deck by the pair $(g,f)$ in lexicographic order, with $g$ the more significant label.

The pair $(g,f)$ is uniform on $ab$ values and independent across cards, so, renaming $(g,f)\\mapsto(g-1)a+f\\in\\{1,\\dots,ab\\}$, this is exactly an inverse $ab$-shuffle. ∎

solutions.title: Reduce to inverse shuffles
solutions.body:
By Problems 16(a) and 16(b), the maximum entropy (standard GSR) $a$-shuffle and the sequential $a$-shuffle have the same transition probabilities $P_a(\sigma\to\tau)$. Let $\bar P_a$ denote the transition probabilities of the inverse $a$-shuffle; Problem 16(c)(iii) says $P_a(\sigma\to\mu)=\bar P_a(\mu\to\sigma)$ for all permutations $\sigma,\mu$.

The probability of reaching $\tau$ from $\sigma$ by an $a$-shuffle and then a $b$-shuffle is $$\sum_\mu P_a(\sigma\to\mu)P_b(\mu\to\tau)=\sum_\mu\bar P_a(\mu\to\sigma)\,\bar P_b(\tau\to\mu).$$ Reading the right side backwards, it is the probability that starting from $\tau$ an inverse $b$-shuffle (to $\mu$) followed by an inverse $a$-shuffle (to $\sigma$) produces $\sigma$. By the product rule (17a), an inverse $b$-shuffle followed by an inverse $a$-shuffle is an inverse $ba$-shuffle, so this equals $\bar P_{ba}(\tau\to\sigma)=\bar P_{ab}(\tau\to\sigma)$, and by 16(c)(iii) again this is $P_{ab}(\sigma\to\tau)$.

So two consecutive shuffles (either form) have the same transition probabilities as one $ab$-shuffle. prompt: **Power Round, Problem 18a.** A *permutation* of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a listing $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ of $1,\dots,n$ in some order. It is also read as an *operation* on ordered listings: $(\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n))$ sends the $\sigma(1)$th element to the first position, the $\sigma(2)$th element to the second position, and so on. Applying it to $(1,2,\dots,n)$ gives the listing $\sigma$ itself; the *identity* $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,n)$ does nothing. The *composition* $\sigma\circ\tau$ is the operation of performing $\tau$ first, then $\sigma$. The *inverse* $\sigma^{-1}$ is the permutation with $\sigma^{-1}\circ\sigma=\mathbf 1$. A *rising sequence* of a permutation $\sigma$ is a maximal sequence of consecutive numbers $k,k+1,\dots,l$ that appear in this order as a subsequence (not necessarily adjacent entries) of $\sigma$. Every permutation decomposes into disjoint rising sequences; for example $(6,1,2,4,7,5,3)$ has the three rising sequences $(1,2,3)$, $(4,5)$, $(6,7)$. For nonnegative integers $j_1+\dots+j_a=n$, the *multinomial coefficient* is $\binom{n}{j_1,\dots,j_a}=\frac{n!}{j_1!\,j_2!\cdots j_a!}$. The *GSR $a$-shuffle* of a deck of $n$ cards numbered $1,\dots,n$ from bottom to top works as follows. *Cutting stage:* cut the deck into $a$ piles (left to right, taking the bottom cards first) of sizes $j_1,\dots,j_a$ (possibly $0$) with $j_1+\dots+j_a=n$, where these sizes occur with probability $\binom{n}{j_1,\dots,j_a}\frac1{a^n}$. *Dropping stage:* drop cards from the bottom of the piles one at a time; if you currently hold piles of sizes $J_1,\dots,J_a$, the next card comes from the $k$th pile with probability $J_k/(J_1+\dots+J_a)$. The order of the cards after dropping, from bottom to top, is read as a permutation of $1,\dots,n$. (The standard GSR shuffle is the case $a=2$.) Suppose $\sigma$ is a permutation with $r$ rising sequences. Prove that the transition probability from $\mathbf 1$ to $\sigma$ for the GSR $a$-shuffle of an $n$-card deck is $$\frac{\binom{a+n-r}{n}}{a^n}.$$

solutions.title: Count paths
solutions.body:
By Problem 15(c) the probability is the number of paths from $\mathbf 1$ to $\sigma$, divided by $a^n$. A path is a cut of $(1,\dots,n)$ into $a$ consecutive (possibly empty) blocks followed by a drop order producing $\sigma$; given the cut, there is at most one drop order (Problem 15(b)), and one exists iff every block, a run of consecutive integers $k,\dots,l$, appears in increasing order in $\sigma$.

A run $k,\dots,l$ appears in order in $\sigma$ iff it contains no 'break' $k'\to k'+1$ with $k'+1$ before $k'$ in $\sigma$; the $r-1$ breaks (positions between consecutive integers) are exactly the boundaries between rising sequences. So the cut must separate at every one of these $r-1$ break positions.

A cut is a multiset of $a-1$ cut positions chosen among the $n+1$ gaps $0,1,\dots,n$ (the block sizes are the differences). It must contain each of the $r-1$ required positions; removing one copy of each leaves an arbitrary multiset of $a-r$ positions among $n+1$, which can be chosen in $\binom{(n+1)+(a-r)-1}{a-r}=\binom{n+a-r}{n}$ ways (and $0$ if $a<r$, consistent with the binomial). So the probability is $\binom{a+n-r}{n}/a^n$. ∎

prompt: **Power Round, Problem 18b.** An *ascent* of a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a position $1\le i<n$ with $\sigma(i)<\sigma(i+1)$; a *descent* is a position $1\le i<n$ with $\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)$ (every position $i<n$ is one or the other). For example, $(2,7,1,3,5,4,8,6)$ has ascents at positions $1,3,4,6$ and descents at $2,5,7$. The *Eulerian number* $\left\langle {n \atop k}\right\rangle$ is the number of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with exactly $k$ ascents. solutions.title: Total probability is 1
solutions.body: Summing over all permutations, $\sum_\sigma\binom{a+n-r(\sigma)}{n}=a^n$. By Problem 10, the number of permutations with $r$ rising sequences equals the number of permutations $\sigma^{-1}$ with $r-1$ descents, i.e. with $n-1-(r-1)=n-r$ ascents: $\left\langle {n \atop n-r}\right\rangle$. solutions.title: Take the limit
solutions.body: By the product rule, $k$ successive $a$-shuffles act as one $a^k$-shuffle. Put $A=a^k$. There are two *perfect riffle shuffles*: cut the deck exactly in half and alternate dropping a card from each half. The *out-shuffle* $O$ drops the original bottom card first and leaves the original top card on top; the *in-shuffle* $I$ drops the original bottom card second. Thus $O(0,1,\dots,2n-1)=0,n,1,n+1,2,n+2,\dots,n-1,2n-1$ and $I(0,1,\dots,2n-1)=n,0,n+1,1,n+2,2,\dots,2n-1,n-1$. We write $O(a_0,\dots,a_{2n-1})$ for $O$ applied to an arbitrary listing, and $O^k$ for $k$ repeated applications (similarly for $I$). The *order* of a shuffle on $2n$ cards is the least positive number of times it must be applied to $0,1,\dots,2n-1$ to return $0,1,\dots,2n-1$. Given a deck of $2n$ cards numbered as usual and $k\in\{0,1,\dots,2n-1\}$, state and prove an algorithm consisting only of in- and out-shuffles for bringing the card numbered $0$ to the $k$th position in the deck. (Hint: consider the binary expansion of $k$.)
answer: Write $k$ in binary; for each bit from the most significant, do an in-shuffle for $1$ and an out-shuffle for $0$

solutions.title: Binary expansion
solutions.body:
*Algorithm.* Write $k=(b_s b_{s-1}\ldots b_0)_2$ with $b_s=1$ (if $k=0$ do nothing). For $i=s,s-1,\dots,0$ in this order perform an in-shuffle if $b_i=1$ and an out-shuffle if $b_i=0$.

*Proof.* A card in position $p<n$ is moved by an out-shuffle to position $2p$ and by an in-shuffle to position $2p+1$ (read off from $O(0,\dots,2n-1)=0,n,1,n+1,\dots$ and $I(0,\dots,2n-1)=n,0,n+1,1,\dots$: the first half of the deck occupies the even positions for $O$ and the odd positions for $I$). Card $0$ starts at position $0$. After the first $t$ operations its position is the number whose binary expansion is $b_sb_{s-1}\ldots b_{s-t+1}$ (each step doubles the position and appends $0$ or $1$). Before the last operation the position is $\lfloor k/2\rfloor\le n-1<n$, and all earlier positions are smaller, so the rules $p\mapsto2p$ and $p\mapsto2p+1$ apply at every step (no reduction modulo $2n-1$ is needed). After all $s+1$ operations the position is $k$. ∎
